questions.q: Split: 'The tall girl with red ribbons skipped to school.'
questions.a: Subject: 'The tall girl with red ribbons' — predicate: 'skipped to school'. A wrong answer making 'girl' alone the subject or 'with red ribbons' the predicate shows the student cuts phrases at word boundaries instead of asking who-did-what.

questions.q: Sentence or fragment: 'Because it was raining very hard.'
questions.a: Fragment — 'because' makes it depend on a main clause that is missing. A wrong answer calling it a sentence reveals the student counts words, not completeness — length does not make a sentence.

questions.q: Which is the complete subject: 'My elder brother, who lives in Delhi, is a doctor.'
questions.a: 'My elder brother, who lives in Delhi,' — the who-clause rides along inside the subject. A wrong answer stopping at 'brother' shows the student hasn't learned a subject can carry its own describing clause.

questions.q: Every English sentence needs two parts that answer two questions: the subject (WHO or WHAT the sentence is about) and the ______ (what the subject DOES or IS).

Fill in the blank: Every English sentence needs two parts that answer two ______: the subject (WHO or WHAT the sentence is about) and the predicate (what the subject DOES or IS). 'The little boy / ran home.' A group of words missing either part is a phrase, not a sentence.
Fill in the blank: Cover the verb: 'The ______ boy ran home' — cover 'ran home'.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can split any simple sentence into subject and predicate, and can tell a complete sentence from a fragment (phrase) every time.
